title: Why are some species immortal?
subtitle: Biology & longevity
subject: sciences
description: Some species seem to defy death. Jellyfish that grow young again, hydras that never age: the secret is cell repair.

hero.hook: Aging is not an absolute law of life. A few species have found the loophole.

blocks.text: We grow old, then we die. Yet the jellyfish [[Turritopsis dohrnii]] can go back to a juvenile stage and start over. A clam named **Ming** lived for **507 years**. So aging is not a universal rule. It is a process that some species get around.
By studying these exceptions, researchers are not chasing science-fiction immortality. They are after the tricks life uses to repair its cells better.
Aging is not only a matter of “wearing out” like a machine. It is an imbalance: damage piles up faster than repairs can fix it.

blocks.caption: Telomeres, at the ends of the chromosomes, shorten with every cell division

blocks.text: At the tips of our chromosomes, the [[telomeres]] work like the plastic ends of a shoelace. Every cell division makes them shorter. Once they are too short, the cell stops dividing. Meanwhile, the body's chemistry produces aggressive molecules that damage proteins and DNA. “Zombie” cells then build up and inflame the tissue around them.

The tardigrade, the tiny “water bear,” can almost switch life off by drying itself out. Its metabolism drops by **99.99%**, and it survives the vacuum of space or extreme radiation without really aging.

Injured or starving, [[Turritopsis dohrnii]] turns its adult cells back into “blank” cells, then becomes a polyp again, its starting stage. That step backward, called transdifferentiation, gives it a form of **biological immortality**.

The **hydra**, a small freshwater polyp, rebuilds its whole body from an almost unlimited stock of [[stem cells]]. It shows no measurable sign of aging. The bowhead whale, for its part, can live past **200 years**, thanks to very efficient DNA repair and strong resistance to cancer.
Lobsters make telomerase all over their body, so their telomeres do not shorten. They keep growing for life and mostly die when molting becomes too costly.

The goal is no longer only to treat Alzheimer's or arthritis one disease at a time, but to attack aging itself. **Senolytics** aim to clear out the zombie cells. In animals, that has already made some functions younger.

Cutting calories without malnutrition also switches on repair pathways, mainly by slowing [[mTOR]], a protein that speeds up growth and sometimes decline. Other labs are trying to “wind the clock back” in cells, the way the jellyfish does, without turning them into tumors.
Even a biologically immortal species dies of predators, disease, or disaster. Death is still an engine of evolution: it makes room for new generations that fit their world better.
For humans, the realistic goal is not to live forever, but to add years **in good health**. And if longevity ever became a technology, it would raise huge questions about fairness and resources.
Biological immortality rests on repairing or resetting cells. The jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii grows young again, and the hydra renews itself without stopping. Aging is not a universal fate.
